name: Sample interview bank
description: An engine sample of the question bank, for checking the Interview practice deck. Each item is adapted from an existing level review and keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: The interviewer: "Write out the numbers 1 to 100. Make me a market on how many 7s you write." Say a fair value and a range. Then work it out.
items.question: How many times does the digit 7 appear?

widget.accept: 20: ten in the units place and ten in the seventies.
widget.label: Count of the digit 7

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the units place and the tens place separately.

byKey.seventy-seven: You counted 77 once. It holds two 7s, one in each place.
byKey.units-only: You counted only the units place: 7, 17, ..., 97. The seventies add ten more in the tens place.

explain.text: The units place shows 7 in 7, 17, ..., 97: ten times. The tens place shows 7 in 70 to 79: ten more, and 77 counts in both. Total 20, which a fair value of about 20 with a range of 15 to 25 would have held.

items.prose: A new game: two dice are rolled, and the contract pays the gap between them, the larger minus the smaller. A gap of $d \ge 1$ happens in $2(6 - d)$ of the 36 rolls.
items.question: What is the fair value? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each gap $d$ by $2(6-d)/36$.

byKey.means: You subtracted the fair values, 3.5 − 3.5. The gap is never negative, so its fair value is above 0.
byKey.one-way: You counted each gap one way round. (1, 3) and (3, 1) both give a gap of 2.

explain.text: Gaps 1 to 5 occur in 10, 8, 6, 4 and 2 rolls. So the fair value is $(10 + 16 + 18 + 16 + 10)/36 = 70/36 = 35/18 \approx 1.94$. A seeded check of 200,000 rolls gives 1.949.

items.prose: The interviewer: how many £1 coins, laid edge to edge, make a mile? A mile is about 1,600 m, and a £1 coin is about 2.3 cm across.
items.question: Which answer would you give?

options.why: You divided metres by centimetres. Convert the mile to 160,000 cm first.
You kept every figure from rough inputs. Give one or two significant figures.
You added two powers of ten. 160,000 ÷ 2.3 is about 70,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put both lengths in centimetres, then divide.

explain.text: A mile is about 160,000 cm, and $160{,}000 / 2.3 \approx 70{,}000$. With the exact figures, 1,609.344 m and 2.25 cm, it is 71,526. One significant figure is the honest answer: about $7 \times 10^4$.

items.prose: Roll three fair dice and be paid the largest face in £.
items.question: What is the fair price? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $P(\max \ge k)$ for each $k$, or count by the largest face.

byKey.two: That is the larger of two dice. A third die pushes the largest up.

explain.text: $P(\max \le k) = (k/6)^3$, so $E[\max] = \sum_{k=1}^{6} P(\max \ge k) = 6 - \tfrac{0 + 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 + 125}{216} = \tfrac{119}{24}$. As a check, the largest face is $k$ in $k^3 - (k - 1)^3$ of the 216 outcomes, which gives the same sum.

items.prose: You ask strangers their birth month, taking each of the 12 months as equally likely.
items.question: How many people do you expect to ask until you have heard every month? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Twelve coupon types: add $12/k$ for $k$ from 1 to 12.

byKey.twelve: You allowed one person per month. Repeats cost extra people.
byKey.square: You gave every month the last stage's wait of 12.

explain.text: Stage $k$ waits $12/(13 - k)$ people, so the total is $12(1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac1{12}) \approx 37.24$. The last month alone takes 12 people on average.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the three terms, then add.

byKey.no-cross: You left out the cross: $5 \times 4 + 8 \times 3 = 44$ tens.
byKey.dropped-carry: You kept the 4 of 44 and dropped its 4 hundreds. 44 tens is 440.

explain.text: $5 \times 3 = 15$, the cross $20 + 24 = 44$, and $8 \times 4 = 32$. Running total: 1,500, then 1,940, then 1,972.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The divisor has four places, so scale both by 10,000.

byKey.down: You worked out $42 \div 7$: the two numbers scaled by different powers.
byKey.up: You worked out $4200 \div 7$: the top scaled once too often.

explain.text: 0.0007 has 4 places, so multiply both by 10,000: $420 \div 7 = 60$. Check: $0.0007 \times 60 = 0.042$.

items.prose: A fair die is rolled three times.
items.question: What is $P(\text{at least one six})$? Give a fraction or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the outcomes with no six first.

byKey.adding: You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ three times. That counts outcomes with two or three sixes more than once.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no six. Take it from 1.
byKey.all: That is three sixes in a row.

explain.text: No six leaves 5 faces per roll: $5^3 = 125$ of the 216 outcomes. So $P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \tfrac{125}{216} = \tfrac{91}{216} \approx 0.4213$.

items.prose: A high-volatility regime persists with chance 0.75 each day.
items.question: How many days does it last on average?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 1 by the daily chance of leaving.

byKey.recip: You used $1/0.75$. Divide by the chance of leaving, 0.25.
byKey.odds: You used $0.75/0.25$, which leaves out the first day.

explain.text: The run length is geometric with exit chance 0.25 a day, so its mean is $1/0.25 = 4$ days.

items.prose: Six colleagues each put their name in a hat and draw one name at random.
items.question: What is the chance that exactly one person draws their own name? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the one person who matches, then count the ways the other five all miss.

byKey.none: That is the chance nobody draws their own name, $\tfrac{265}{720}$.
byKey.e: That is the large-$n$ limit $1/e$. For six people count exactly.
byKey.sixth: That is one person's chance of a match, ignoring whether the others miss.

explain.text: Pick the matching person in 6 ways. The other five must all miss: 44 ways, as for five hats. So $264/720 \approx 0.3667$.
